lesson.title: Seeing Your Own Feelings in Everyone Else
lesson.summary: Projection is unconsciously attributing your own unacceptable thoughts, feelings, or impulses to someone else, so an uncomfortable truth about yourself becomes a claim about another person instead.
lesson.body:
Where denial rejects a fact about the world, projection does something more elaborate. It takes a feeling or impulse that actually belongs to the person and unconsciously relocates it onto someone else. Instead of thinking "I feel hostile toward you," which might be too uncomfortable or unacceptable to admit even to oneself, the mind flips it around to "you are being hostile toward me." The feeling does not go away, it just changes address.

Consider a student who is quietly jealous of a classmate's success on a project. Admitting to jealousy feels petty and uncomfortable, so instead the student becomes convinced that the classmate is the jealous, small-minded one, and starts complaining to friends about how competitive and insecure this classmate seems. Or consider someone who is tempted to be unfaithful in a relationship. Rather than face that uncomfortable impulse in themselves, they become suspicious and accusatory, certain that their own partner is the one being unfaithful, often with little real evidence.

Why does this work as a defense? Attributing an unwanted feeling to somebody else is, in an odd way, more comfortable than owning it. It lets the person avoid the guilt or shame of the impulse while still, at some level, expressing and reacting to it, just at a safer distance. This is also the conceptual seed behind projective personality tests, covered in a later chapter, which are built on the idea that people will unconsciously project their inner thoughts and feelings onto ambiguous material like inkblots.

It is easy to confuse projection with simple hypocrisy or with denial, so it is worth being precise. Denial says a painful fact is not true. Projection does not deny the feeling exists, it just insists the feeling belongs to somebody else. If denial is "this isn't happening," projection is closer to "I don't feel that way, but you clearly do."
